title: Changes in reading habits
subject: reading

paragraphs.text: What are the implications of the way we read today?

Look around on your next plane trip. The iPad is the new pacifier for babies and toddlers. Younger school-aged children read stories on smartphones; older kids don’t read at all, but hunch over video games. Parents and other passengers read on tablets or skim a flotilla of email and news feeds. Unbeknown to most of us, an invisible, game-changing transformation links everyone in this picture: the neuronal circuit that underlies the brain’s ability to read is subtly, rapidly changing and this has implications for everyone from the pre-reading toddler to the expert adult.

As work in neurosciences indicates, the acquisition of literacy necessitated a new circuit in our species’ brain more than 6,000 years ago. That circuit evolved from a very simple mechanism for decoding basic information, like the number of goats in one’s herd, to the present, highly elaborated reading brain. My research depicts how the present reading brain enables the development of some of our most important intellectual and affective processes: internalized knowledge, analogical reasoning, and inference; perspective-taking and empathy; critical analysis and the generation of insight. Research surfacing in many parts of the world now cautions that each of these essential ‘deep reading’ processes may be under threat as we move into digital-based modes of reading.

This is not a simple, binary issue of print versus digital reading and technological innovation. As MIT scholar Sherry Turkle has written, we do not err as a society when we innovate but when we ignore what we disrupt or diminish while innovating. In this hinge moment between print and digital cultures, society needs to confront what is diminishing in the expert reading circuit, what our children and older students are not developing, and what we can do about it.

We know from research that the reading circuit is not given to human beings through a genetic blueprint like vision or language; it needs an environment to develop. Further, it will adapt to that environment’s requirements – from different writing systems to the characteristics of whatever medium is used. If the dominant medium advantages processes that are fast, multi-task oriented and well-suited for large volumes of information, like the current digital medium, so will the reading circuit. As UCLA psychologist Patricia Greenfield writes, the result is that less attention and time will be allocated to slower, time-demanding deep reading processes.

Increasing reports from educators and from researchers in psychology and the humanities bear this out. English literature scholar and teacher Mark Edmundson describes how many college students actively avoid the classic literature of the 19th and 20th centuries in favour of something simpler as they no longer have the patience to read longer, denser, more difficult texts. We should be less concerned with students’ ‘cognitive impatience’, however, than by what may underlie it: the potential inability of large numbers of students to read with a level of critical analysis sufficient to comprehend the complexity of thought and argument found in more demanding texts.

Multiple studies show that digital screen use may be causing a variety of troubling downstream effects on reading comprehension in older high school and college students. In Stavanger, Norway, psychologist Anne Mangen and her colleagues studied how high school students comprehend the same material in different mediums. Mangen’s group asked subjects questions about a short story whose plot had universal student appeal; half of the students read the story on a tablet, the other half in paperback. Results indicated that students who read on print were superior in their comprehension to screen-reading peers, particularly in their ability to sequence detail and reconstruct the plot in chronological order.

Ziming Liu from San Jose State University has conducted a series of studies which indicate that the ‘new norm’ in reading is skimming, involving word-spotting and browsing through the text. Many readers now use a pattern when reading in which they sample the first line and then word-spot through the rest of the text. When the reading brain skims like this, it reduces time allocated to deep reading processes. In other words, we don’t have time to grasp complexity, to understand another’s feelings, to perceive beauty, and to create thoughts of the reader’s own.

The possibility that critical analysis, empathy and other deep reading processes could become the unintended ‘collateral damage’ of our digital culture is not a straightforward binary issue about print versus digital reading. It is about how we all have begun to read on various mediums and how that changes not only what we read, but also the purposes for which we read. Nor is it only about the young. The subtle atrophy of critical analysis and empathy affects us all equally. It affects our ability to navigate a constant bombardment of information. It incentivizes a retreat to the most familiar stores of unchecked information, which require and receive no analysis, leaving us susceptible to false information and irrational ideas.

There’s an old rule in neuroscience that does not alter with age: use it or lose it. It is a very hopeful principle when applied to critical thought in the reading brain because it implies choice. The story of the changing reading brain is hardly finished. We possess both the science and the technology to identify and redress the changes in how we read before they become entrenched. If we work to understand exactly what we will lose, alongside the extraordinary new capacities that the digital world has brought us, there is as much reason for excitement as caution.

groups.instruction:
Questions 14–17

Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s main point in the first paragraph?

options.text: Our use of technology is having a hidden effect on us.
Technology can be used to help youngsters to read.
Travellers should be encouraged to use technology on planes.
Playing games is a more popular use of technology than reading.

questions.explanation:
译文：作者在第一段的主要观点是什么？

在选择题中会经常遇到关于“某一段主要观点、主要思想、段落主旨”的问题。这种问题虽然定位清晰，比如本题直接告诉考生去第一段找答案，但是难点在于这类题目往往难以通过某一句话来确定答案。因此对于这篇文章，我们采用平行阅读的思路，直接通读，用最快的方式去掌握每一句话的“用意”，来协助总结段落主要观点。本段前四句话是在向读者呈现当今不同年龄层的人们的阅读方式，而最后一句话，也是本段最长的一句话，是在进行总结“我们大多数人都不知道的是，这种无形的、改变游戏规则的变革将以上这幅画面中的每一个人都联系在了一起：构建人脑阅读能力的神经元回路正在微妙且快速地发生变化，以及这对每一个人都在产生影响，无论是处于预读期的婴幼儿还是专业的成年阅读者。”很显然，我们的答案出自这句话。

然后我们再来看一下选项。

选项A：Our use of technology is having a hidden effect on us. 对于科技的使用已经对我们的生活有了隐隐的影响。

选项B：Technology can be used to help youngsters to read. 科技可以用于帮助年轻人阅读。

选项C：Travellers should be encouraged to use technology on planes. 应该鼓励旅行者在飞机上使用科技产品。

选项D：Playing games is a more popular use of technology than reading. 科技在游戏产业里比在阅读中应用得更广泛。

通过对于四个选项的分析，我们可以很明显地看出B、C、D选项都是相对具体的例子，也对应了第一段前四句话中提到的几类人群。而A选项是相对提炼、总结性的观点，对应原文段落的最后一句话，表明这些科技的变革让构建人脑阅读能力的神经元回路快速发生变化，并且对每一个人都在产生影响。因此答案为A。

questions.prompt: What main point does Sherry Turkle make about innovation?

options.text: Technological innovation has led to a reduction in print reading.
We should pay attention to what might be lost when innovation occurs.
We should encourage more young people to become involved in innovation.
There is a difference between developing products and developing ideas.

questions.explanation:
译文：Sherry Turkle对于变革的主要观点是什么？

这道题目问到了具体某个人的观点，所以可以通过人名信息进行定位。原文说Sherry提到对于社会而言，我们的创新并没有错，而是错在创新过程中人们会忽视那些被破坏或削弱的事物。

选项A：Technological innovation has led to a reduction in print reading. 科技变革导致了纸质阅读的减少。

选项B：We should pay attention to what might be lost when innovation occurs. 我们应该多关注在变革发生时那些可能会消失的事物。

选项C：We should encourage more young people to become involved in innovation. 我们应该鼓励年轻人多参与到变革中。

选项D：There is a difference between developing products and developing ideas. 产品的发展和思想的发展有区别。

原文中并列使用disrupt和diminish两个词来告诉读者变革引发的问题，虽然有考生可能对于这两个词并不熟悉，但是我们知道dis作为前缀表示否定，而minish表示缩小，所以可以推测该词是“逐渐缩减、消失”的意思，刚好对应B项中的lost。原文中虽有提到这是一个印刷文化和数字文化交融的转折期，提到了现在的科技变革带来了阅读脑回路的减少，但是并没有提到是科技导致了纸质阅读的减少，所以A选项不对。而对于年轻人也只是提到我们要多去关注这些成长中未发展的部分并采取措施，所以C、D两项并不正确。

questions.prompt: What point is the writer making in the fourth paragraph?

options.text: Humans have an inborn ability to read and write.
Reading can be done using many different mediums.
Writing systems make unexpected demands on the brain.
Some brain circuits adjust to whatever is required of them.

questions.explanation:
译文：作者在第四段的主要观点是什么？

本题的原文定位方式和14题类似，由于题目直接给出了段落信息，所以考生可以直接进行阅读。

选项A：Humans have an inborn ability to read and write. 人类具有与生俱来的阅读和书写能力。

选项B：Reading can be done using many different mediums. 阅读可以通过多种不同的方式进行。

选项C：Writing systems make unexpected demands on the brain.书写系统对于大脑有出乎意料的要求。

选项D：Some brain circuits adjust to whatever is required of them. 一些大脑的回路会根据需要进行适应调整。

段落的第一句就提到阅读回路（reading circuit）不是通过基因直接赋予人类的，所以可以快速排除A选项中的与生俱来（inborn）。随后文中提到，这些回路需要环境来发展，并且（further）会根据环境的条件需要进行适应调节（adapt to），对应D选项。到此，可以得知D项为正确答案。再看B、C选项中提到的阅读方式和写作系统，这两个点在原文中虽有提及：from different writing systems to the characteristics of whatever medium is used，但是这个部分在段落中是作为例证出现的，进一步说明阅读回路会根据环境要求来进行调节，并非作者的主要观点，因此排除。

questions.prompt: According to Mark Edmundson, the attitude of college students

options.text: has changed the way he teaches.
has influenced what they select to read.
does not worry him as much as it does others.
does not match the views of the general public.

questions.explanation:
译文：根据Mark Edmundson，大学生的态度

此题的原文定位方式和15题类似，所以可以通过人名快速定位到第五段的第二句话。Mark老师提到大学生对于晦涩的19和20世纪文学的抵触，以及对于简单文学作品的喜好。而造成这个的原因是什么呢？考生可以看到第五段第一句话bear this out中的this，在英文正式文体中，指代是非常常用的写作手法，而这里的this指代的就是上一段中提到的关于科技变革带来的阅读习惯的改变，所以对应选项B。

选项A：has changed the way he teaches. 改变了他的教学方式。

选项B：has influenced what they select to read. 影响了他们选择阅读的内容。

选项C：does not worry him as much as it does others. 并没有让他像别人一样有太多的担忧。

选项D：does not match the views of the general public. 与大众的观点不吻合。

我们再来看另外的三个选项错在哪里。原文并没有提到关于教学方法方式的任何信息，所以可以很快排除A选项。而C选项是在针对第五段第三句话中的 we should be less concerned with students来迷惑考生，通过句型分析我们可以得知，however后面的部分是concern的核心，是“认知焦躁”表象下的潜在问题，所以排除C。D选项也是原文中没有提到的，因此排除。

groups.contextHtml:
Studies on digital screen use

There have been many studies on digital screen use, showing some [18] ______ trends. Psychologist Anne Mangen gave high-school students a short story to read, half using digital and half using print mediums. Her team then used a question-and-answer technique to find out how [19] ______  each group’s understanding of the plot was. The findings showed a clear pattern in the responses, with those who read screens finding the order of information [20] ______  to recall.

Studies by Ziming Liu show that students are tending to read [21] ______  words and phrases in a text to save time. This approach, she says, gives the reader a superficial understanding of the [22] ______  content of material, leaving no time for thought.

groups.instruction:
Questions 23–26

Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 2?

In questions 23–26 on your answer sheet, choose

YES if the statement agrees with the views of the writer

NO if the statement contradicts the views of the writer

NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

questions.prompt: The medium we use to read can affect our choice of reading content.
questions.explanation:
译文：我们阅读的方式会对我们选择的阅读内容有所影响。

根据平行阅读法的方式，我们可以将这道题目的原文定位锁定在第八段。然后可以看到这一段的第二句话开始讲“我们的阅读方式改变着我们阅读的内容（what we read）以及我们阅读的目的（the purposes for which we read），而这句话开头的It指代前文提到的数字化时代，因此本题为YES。

questions.prompt: Some age groups are more likely to lose their complex reading skills than others.
questions.explanation:
译文：一些年龄群体的人会比另外一些人更容易失去综合阅读技能。

这道题目仅需要看到age groups，再回到原文看到the young，就可以定位到答案位置。即使考生不认识atrophy，也可以根据equally（平等地，同样地）得出答案，这种影响对于不同年龄群体的影响并没有因人而异，因此答案为NO。

questions.prompt: False information has become more widespread in today’s digital era.
questions.explanation:
译文：在现今的数字化时代，虚假信息已经变得更普遍。

通过题干关键词false information（虚假信息）可以快速定位到原文的位置。虽然原文中出现了对应的false information，但是并没有提到是否在如今的数字化时代变得更加普遍，因此可以得出结论为NOT GIVEN。

questions.prompt: We still have opportunities to rectify the problems that technology is presenting.
questions.explanation:
译文：我们仍有机会去纠正科技目前带来的问题。

本题定位到文章的最后一段，但是部分考生也许不认识题干词rectify（纠正）。但是通过原文最后一段以及题干的主体部分“我们仍有机会去……科技带来的问题”，可以推测这句话的含义应该是正面的作用，比如“改正问题、减少问题”等等。然后回到原文中说的“我们拥有科学和技术来识别和纠正在这种阅读方法扎根之前所发生的变化”，因此可以明白，对于“问题”我们是有方法和机会去解决的，所以得出答案为YES。

articleHtml:
Changes in reading habits

What are the implications of the way we read today?

 

Look around on your next plane trip. The iPad is the new pacifier for babies and toddlers. Younger school-aged children read stories on smartphones; older kids don’t read at all, but hunch over video games. Parents and other passengers read on tablets or skim a flotilla of email and news feeds. Unbeknown to most of us, an invisible, game-changing transformation links everyone in this picture: the neuronal circuit that underlies the brain’s ability to read is subtly, rapidly changing and this has implications for everyone from the pre-reading toddler to the expert adult.

 

As work in neurosciences indicates, the acquisition of literacy necessitated a new circuit in our species’ brain more than 6,000 years ago. That circuit evolved from a very simple mechanism for decoding basic information, like the number of goats in one’s herd, to the present, highly elaborated reading brain. My research depicts how the present reading brain enables the development of some of our most important intellectual and affective processes: internalized knowledge, analogical reasoning, and inference; perspective-taking and empathy; critical analysis and the generation of insight. Research surfacing in many parts of the world now cautions that each of these essential ‘deep reading’ processes may be under threat as we move into digital-based modes of reading.

 

This is not a simple, binary issue of print versus digital reading and technological innovation. As MIT scholar Sherry Turkle has written, we do not err as a society when we innovate but when we ignore what we disrupt or diminish while innovating. In this hinge moment between print and digital cultures, society needs to confront what is diminishing in the expert reading circuit, what our children and older students are not developing, and what we can do about it.

 

We know from research that the reading circuit is not given to human beings through a genetic blueprint like vision or language; it needs an environment to develop. Further, it will adapt to that environment’s requirements – from different writing systems to the characteristics of whatever medium is used. If the dominant medium advantages processes that are fast, multi-task oriented and well-suited for large volumes of information, like the current digital medium, so will the reading circuit. As UCLA psychologist Patricia Greenfield writes, the result is that less attention and time will be allocated to slower, time-demanding deep reading processes.

 

Increasing reports from educators and from researchers in psychology and the humanities bear this out. English literature scholar and teacher Mark Edmundson describes how many college students actively avoid the classic literature of the 19th and 20th centuries in favour of something simpler as they no longer have the patience to read longer, denser, more difficult texts. We should be less concerned with students’ ‘cognitive impatience’, however, than by what may underlie it: the potential inability of large numbers of students to read with a level of critical analysis sufficient to comprehend the complexity of thought and argument found in more demanding texts.

 

Multiple studies show that digital screen use may be causing a variety of troubling downstream effects on reading comprehension in older high school and college students. In Stavanger, Norway, psychologist Anne Mangen and her colleagues studied how high school students comprehend the same material in different mediums. Mangen’s group asked subjects questions about a short story whose plot had universal student appeal; half of the students read the story on a tablet, the other half in paperback. Results indicated that students who read on print were superior in their comprehension to screen-reading peers, particularly in their ability to sequence detail and reconstruct the plot in chronological order.

 

Ziming Liu from San Jose State University has conducted a series of studies which indicate that the ‘new norm’ in reading is skimming, involving word-spotting and browsing through the text. Many readers now use a pattern when reading in which they sample the first line and then word-spot through the rest of the text. When the reading brain skims like this, it reduces time allocated to deep reading processes. In other words, we don’t have time to grasp complexity, to understand another’s feelings, to perceive beauty, and to create thoughts of the reader’s own.

 

The possibility that critical analysis, empathy and other deep reading processes could become the unintended ‘collateral damage’ of our digital culture is not a straightforward binary issue about print versus digital reading. It is about how we all have begun to read on various mediums and how that changes not only what we read, but also the purposes for which we read. Nor is it only about the young. The subtle atrophy of critical analysis and empathy affects us all equally. It affects our ability to navigate a constant bombardment of information. It incentivizes a retreat to the most familiar stores of unchecked information, which require and receive no analysis, leaving us susceptible to false information and irrational ideas.

 

There’s an old rule in neuroscience that does not alter with age: use it or lose it. It is a very hopeful principle when applied to critical thought in the reading brain because it implies choice. The story of the changing reading brain is hardly finished. We possess both the science and the technology to identify and redress the changes in how we read before they become entrenched. If we work to understand exactly what we will lose, alongside the extraordinary new capacities that the digital world has brought us, there is as much reason for excitement as caution.
